summary.text: Polarization is a property of transverse waves that describes the geometric direction in which the oscillations point.
In a transverse wave the wiggle is perpendicular to the direction of travel, so sound in air or liquid, which moves along its travel direction, cannot be polarized.
Light can be linearly, circularly or elliptically polarized, and a polarizer passes only one polarization, turning unpolarized light into polarized light.

facts.label: Requirement
facts.value: The wave must be transverse; longitudinal ones cannot be polarized

facts.label: Unpolarized sources
facts.value: The sun, flames and incandescent lamps

facts.label: By reflection
facts.value: Light bouncing off a surface at an angle becomes partly polarized

facts.label: Photon view
facts.value: Polarization comes from photon spin, right or left handed

items.prompt: A guitar string can be plucked up and down, side to side, or at an angle. What does this show about the string's waves?

options.label: Their oscillation direction can vary, which is what polarization describes
They are longitudinal waves that travel along the string
They always vibrate vertically unless damped
Their frequency changes with the plucking direction

items.explain: The vibrations can be vertical, horizontal or anywhere between, which is the geometric orientation that polarization specifies.

items.prompt: Why can sound traveling through air not be polarized the way light can?

options.label: Its frequency is too low for the effect to appear
It needs a material medium to travel through
Its particles move along the travel direction, not across it
It is too weak for any instrument to measure

items.explain: In longitudinal waves such as sound in a gas, the displacement is always in the direction of propagation, so there is no polarization.

items.prompt: Light straight from a candle flame passes through a polarizing filter. What comes out the other side?

options.label: Unpolarized light, unchanged
Light of one polarization only
No light at all
Circularly polarized light only

items.explain: Flames give an equal mixture of polarizations, and a polarizer lets through only one, producing polarized light.

items.prompt: Glare bounces off a lake at a slant. How does that light differ from direct sunlight?

options.label: It is partially polarized
It is entirely unpolarized
It is entirely circularly polarized
It has lost all its energy

items.explain: Light becomes partially polarized when it reflects at an angle from a surface.

items.prompt: A beam's fields rotate steadily around its direction of travel. What kind of polarization is this?

options.label: Linear polarization, with fields in one fixed direction
No polarization, since the beam is a plain stream
A longitudinal wave, like sound in the air
Circular or elliptical polarization

items.explain: In circular or elliptical polarization the fields rotate at a constant rate, right-handed or left-handed.

items.prompt: In the photon picture, what is a circularly polarized beam made of?

options.label: Photons that all have the same spin, right or left
A random mix of right and left spins
Photons that carry no spin of any kind
Photons held in a superposition of both spins

items.explain: Circularly polarized waves consist of photons with only one type of spin, while linearly polarized waves are a superposition of both.

paragraphs.heading: Which way the wave shakes
paragraphs.text: Polarization is a property of transverse waves that describes the direction in which they oscillate. In a transverse wave, the oscillation is perpendicular to the direction the wave travels. A taut string, such as a guitar string, is a good example. Depending on how it is plucked, it can vibrate up and down, side to side, or in any direction in between.

paragraphs.heading: Waves that cannot be polarized
paragraphs.text: Longitudinal waves are different. In sound waves in a liquid or gas, the particles always move along the direction the wave is going, so these waves show no polarization. Transverse waves that do show it include light, radio waves, gravitational waves, and shear waves, which are transverse sound waves in solids.

paragraphs.heading: The fields inside light
paragraphs.text: A light wave is made of an electric field and a magnetic field that oscillate together and are always perpendicular to each other. By convention, the polarization direction is the direction of the electric field. In linear polarization, each field oscillates in a single direction. In circular or elliptical polarization, the fields rotate at a steady rate around the beam's direction of travel. The rotation can be right-handed or left-handed.

paragraphs.heading: Making polarized light
paragraphs.text: Light from the sun, from flames and from incandescent lamps is made of short wave trains with an equal mix of polarizations; this is called unpolarized light. A polarizer lets through waves of only one polarization, so passing unpolarized light through it gives polarized light. The most common optical materials leave polarization alone. Materials that show birefringence, dichroism or optical activity, though, treat light differently depending on its polarization, and some are used to make polarizing filters. Light also becomes partly polarized when it reflects off a surface at an angle.

paragraphs.heading: The photon picture
paragraphs.text: Quantum mechanics also lets us treat light as a stream of particles called photons. Seen this way, polarization is set by a property of photons called spin. A photon spins either right-handed or left-handed about its direction of travel. Circularly polarized waves are made of photons with just one kind of spin. Linearly polarized waves are made of photons in a superposition of the right and left states, with equal amplitudes and phases lined up so the wave oscillates in a plane.

paragraphs.heading: Where it matters
paragraphs.text: Polarization is an important quantity in sciences dealing with transverse waves, for example optics, seismology, radio and microwaves. Technologies that depend on it especially include lasers, radar, and wireless and optical fiber telecommunications. Most light sources are incoherent and unpolarized, or only partly polarized. That is because they give out a random mixture of waves with different frequencies, phases and polarization states.
